name: Platelet-rich fibrin for hair

lead: Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) is made by spinning your own blood to form a platelet- and white-cell-rich fibrin clot, a relative of PRP. People try it on the scalp hoping for thicker-looking hair.

The platelets in the clot release growth factors such as PDGF, TGF-beta and VEGF, and the fibrin acts as a scaffold near follicles. PRF is documented mainly in dental and oral surgery; for hair, one small registered trial of 10 participants compares it with PRP in female pattern hair loss, with no results published.

paras: It is an in-clinic procedure: blood is drawn, spun into a clot, and the material is placed in the scalp, much like PRP sessions. It is offered as an off-label aesthetic treatment, usually as a series of visits.
It is an injection-based procedure using your own blood. Risks specific to hair use are not described in published sources, and it is off-label for hair.

angle.text: Users and clinics try PRF on thinning scalp hair as a relative of PRP, hoping growth factors released near the follicles will thicken hair. It is documented mainly in dentistry, and one small registered trial has looked at hair.

lead: Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) is a preparation made by spinning a person's own blood in a centrifuge, without the anticoagulants used for platelet-rich plasma (PRP), to produce a platelet- and white-cell-rich fibrin matrix.[1][2][3] For hair, a liquid injectable version (i-PRF) is placed into the scalp, with the aim of delivering growth factors to thinning follicles so hair looks thicker and fuller.[1][4]

PRF is a derivative of PRP and is documented mainly in dentistry and oral surgery, where it is used for periodontal and extraction-socket healing; the liquid injectable form became available in 2014, and reviews now list facial aesthetics and hair regrowth among its uses.[1][5][6] People interested in non-surgical hair thickening treat PRF as an alternative to PRP, in some cases because its fibrin matrix is described as releasing growth factors more slowly.[1][7]

Studies in androgenetic alopecia are small but growing. A 2024 review found five clinical studies showing benefit; a 2026 multicenter randomized trial in women compared PRP, i-PRF and concentrated growth factors; and a 2026 systematic review pooled 20 regenerative-medicine studies in androgenetic alopecia, including PRF.[7][8][9]
infobox: Injectable PRF (i-PRF), introduced as a liquid form in 2014[1]

paras: Blood is drawn and centrifuged, and the protocol matters: reviews describe how g-force, timing, tube surface and anticoagulant use change the platelet and growth-factor content of the product.[2][10] A classification system sorts platelet concentrates by leukocyte and fibrin content into pure PRP, leukocyte-rich PRP, pure PRF and leukocyte- and platelet-rich fibrin (L-PRF, associated with Choukroun's PRF).[3]

Until 2014 PRF was available clinically only as a solid clot; changes to centrifugation and tube technology produced the liquid injectable version, i-PRF.[1] A 2024 narrative review of PRF in androgenetic alopecia reports no consensus on preparation protocols.[7]

For hair, i-PRF is injected into the scalp, including by mesotherapy gun in one case series.[11] Beyond pattern hair loss, case reports describe PRF in cicatricial alopecia from discoid lupus and as scalp preparation with stromal vascular fraction before a hair transplant in a patient with lichen planus.[12][13]
A systematic review of injectable PRF across alopecia and facial rejuvenation covered seven studies in 130 patients, and three alopecia studies reported improved hair density and growth.[14]

Because PRF is made from the patient's own blood, reviews generally describe adverse events as minor. A case series of 11 women reported only minor, self-limited adverse effects, and a 30-patient study reported minimal adverse reactions.[11][4] In the multicenter trial, i-PRF had the lowest adverse event rate of the three preparations compared.[8]

A prospective single-center study of 30 patients with androgenetic alopecia who had not responded adequately to conventional treatment gave six monthly i-PRF injections and reported an 80% response rate at six months, with improved hair scores and scalp symptoms.[4] An 11-woman case series in female pattern hair loss reported improved follicle density, hair volume and thickness, and patient scores.[11]

A 2026 multicenter randomized trial of 74 completers compared PRP, i-PRF and concentrated growth factors over four sessions in female pattern hair loss; CGF and i-PRF produced larger hair count increases than PRP.[8] A 2026 PRISMA systematic review of 20 studies and 724 patients across five regenerative modalities reported fast, consistent density gains with PRF, along with heterogeneous protocols and limited long-term data.[9] A 2023 trial registration lists a 10-participant comparison of PRF and PRP in female pattern hair loss.[15]

timeline.event: Liquid injectable PRF (i-PRF) becomes available through modified centrifugation and tube technology.[1]
Reviews and a case series on injectable PRF for hair loss are published.[7][11][14]
Multicenter randomized trial comparing PRP, i-PRF and CGF in female pattern hair loss, and a systematic review of regenerative therapies including PRF.[8][9]
